segments.t: This is Kukhnya, a Russian comedy set in the kitchen of Claude Monet, a smart restaurant in Moscow, where the chef, Barinov, shouts and young Max cooks. This episode is about bets: the chef gambles on football, and Max gets a surprise that frightens him. It opens away from the kitchen, in an ordinary flat late at night, where a boy creeps in and his mother whispers about his father's luck. You'll hear it in Russian first, and you don't need to catch every word.
Извини, мама, я сильно опоздал сегодня.
Почему ты пришёл так поздно домой?
Я долго гулял с моими друзьями.
А папа разве сердится на меня?
Папа опять проиграл все наши деньги.
Он снова играл на наши деньги?
Да, он делал ставки на футбол.
И его любимая команда опять проиграла?
Да, его любимый Спартак снова проиграл.
Теперь у нас совсем нет денег?
Ничего, сынок, мы со всем справимся.
Я завтра найду себе хорошую работу.
Извини, мама, я сильно опоздал сегодня.

'Sorry, mom, I was very late today.' The way to express 'sorry' marks the casual form, said to one person you know well. The action The way to express 'was late' takes a he-word past time frame ending since he is a boy. And The way to express 'strongly' stands where English says "very".
Почему ты пришёл так поздно домой?
'Why did you come home so late?' 'to home' is used here is one little word that already carries the "to". "At home" is a different word. The action word means "came", on foot.
Я долго гулял с моими друзьями.
'I walked for a long time with my friends.' The action word means to stroll or hang about, not to walk somewhere. "With my friends" uses a matching ending on both words after the connecting word.
'You got lucky that dad is sleeping.' Russian doesn't say "you got lucky". It says "to you it was lucky", so luck happens to you. The last action word means "is sleeping". She is on his side.
А папа разве сердится на меня?
'Is dad really angry with me?' The word at the start means "really?", a bit of doubt. Russians are angry "on" someone, using a self-directed ending.
Папа опять проиграл все наши деньги.
'Dad lost all our money again.' The action word is "played", with a starting bit in front, so it's "played away": you lose by playing. We hear 'money' is multiple, so "all" uses the multiple form.
Он снова играл на наши деньги?
'Did he play with our money again?' Russians play "on money", meaning for stakes. When they say 'again' is a twin of the one from his mother's line.
Да, он делал ставки на футбол.
'Yes, he placed bets on football.' Russians "make" a bet. Notice the part 'bet' is something you put down, from the action word "to put". And it's "on football".
И его любимая команда опять проиграла?
'And his favorite team lost again?' In Russian, 'team' translates is she-word, so "favourite" and "lost" take matching she-word endings. The question is short and weary.
Да, его любимый Спартак снова проиграл.

'Yes, his favorite Spartak lost again.' Spartak is a Moscow football club, and the chef in this show is a fan too. Now the descriptive words and action words have he-word forms with no she-word endings, because Spartak is a he-word.
Теперь у нас совсем нет денег?
'Now do we have no money at all?' It literally says "at us entirely no of money". After "no", The way to express 'money' takes a genitive ending. There is no "have" and no "any", just that ending.
Ничего, сынок, мы со всем справимся.

'It is alright, son, we will cope with everything.' 'nothing' is used here is Russian for "never mind" here. 'son' is used here takes a fond diminutive form. "We will cope" is the Russian word Louis used in the pastry kitchen.
Я завтра найду себе хорошую работу.

'Tomorrow I will find myself a good job.' It says "will find to myself". Listen to how 'job' takes an object ending, because it's the thing he will find. He says it with a boy's confidence. Now let's hear it once more, start to finish.
